articles.title: France's €20.35B 4→3 Mobile Deal Has Four Days to Close
articles.subtitle: The SFR consortium faces a June 5 hard deadline — a miss triggers bondholder pressure on Altice France's €40B+ debt pile.
articles.body_md:
The most consequential moment in the European telecom consolidation wave arrives on **June 5**. **Bouygues Telecom** (42%, ~€8.5B), **Free-Iliad** (31%, ~€6.3B), and **Orange** (27%, ~€5.5B) have until that date to convert four months of exclusivity negotiations into a binding agreement to acquire **Altice France**'s **SFR** assets for **€20.35B** — a figure raised 20% from the **€17B** initial bid rejected in October 2025, and unchanged since.

This is the second extension. The original May 15 deadline passed without a signed deal; official statements from all three buyers carry explicit "no certainty" language. The structural deal logic has not shifted: Orange acquires SFR's fixed broadband and B2B network assets, Bouygues absorbs mobile and rural coverage obligations, and Free-Iliad retains spectrum blocks and overlap assets. What has not been resolved is the operational complexity of carving SFR's integrated infrastructure — towers, MVNO contracts, wholesale agreements, and fibre assets — across three simultaneous buyers in a single closing.

## The Regulatory Clock Has Not Started

The **Autorité de la concurrence** has not been formally notified. Under French competition law, the merger review clock does not begin until notification, which requires a binding signed agreement — meaning Phase 1 (typically 25 working days) cannot begin at all until a deal is signed. This timeline compression matters: if June 5 passes unsigned, a third extension would materially elevate pressure on **Altice France**'s bondholder structure. **Patrick Drahi**'s group carries a **€40B+** debt load at the Altice France holding level, creating both an incentive to transact and a ceiling on how much further negotiation the sellers can sustain.

## Regulatory Backdrop Has Improved

The **European Commission**'s April 30 Draft Revised Merger Guidelines — covered separately this edition — directly improve the regulatory environment for the deal. By abandoning the rigid 2-year horizon for assessing merger investment benefits, the Commission has materially lowered the analytical burden for defending 4→3 mobile market consolidation in Brussels. The Autorité de la concurrence runs its own review process under the EU framework, but the signal from the Commission on infrastructure merger logic is unambiguous.

This deal, if signed, would reshape French mobile competition for a decade. The consumer and wholesale market remedies — spectrum sharing, MVNO access, rural coverage obligations — will be as consequential as the headline price.

**Watch over the next 6–18 months:** June 5 outcome is the immediate signal. A signed deal triggers a 25-working-day Phase 1 clock; possible Phase 2 referral if remedies around MVNO access or spectrum reallocation are contested. A third extension or withdrawal would put SFR's future structurally in question and likely trigger bondholder negotiations at Altice France — making France's third-largest mobile operator unpredictable for 12–18 months following any deal collapse.
articles.summary: The €20.35B consortium offer for SFR — led by Bouygues, Free-Iliad, and Orange — faces a June 5 exclusivity deadline, the second extension since the original May 15 date. A failure to sign would increase pressure on Altice France's €40B+ debt load and risk unravelling the largest active European telecom M&A transaction.

articles.title: EU Rewrites Merger Rules — Telecom 4→3 Deals Get a Structural Tailwind
articles.subtitle: The Commission's first merger overhaul in two decades scraps the 2-year benefit horizon that blocked infrastructure M&A for a generation.
articles.body_md:
The **European Commission** published Draft Revised Merger Guidelines on **April 30, 2026** — the first consolidation of EU merger control guidance in over two decades. The prior horizontal guidelines dated from **2004**; non-horizontal guidelines from **2008**. The revision is not administrative. It directly addresses the analytical framework that has constrained capital-intensive infrastructure mergers, and its publication coincides precisely with the active phase of Europe's most consequential telecom consolidation wave.

## The Critical Change: Investment Benefits Horizon

The most consequential provision for telecom, energy, and digital infrastructure deals is the abandonment of the **rigid 2-year horizon** for assessing merger investment benefits. Under the old framework, merging parties were required to demonstrate that claimed efficiencies — including network investment commitments — would materialise within two years of deal close. For infrastructure sectors with capital expenditure cycles running **5–10 years**, this was an effectively impossible evidentiary standard: it required implausible near-term construction timelines and penalised exactly the long-horizon investment rationales that regulators in the UK, US, and Asia have increasingly encouraged.

The new framework permits proportionate evidence of medium-term investment benefits, directly lowering the analytical burden for the **SFR** France 4→3 transaction, the reported **Deutsche Telekom / T-Mobile US** combination, and any forthcoming Nordic or Southern European consolidation.

## A New Theory of Harm: Investment Competition

The Commission has simultaneously codified **"loss of investment competition"** as a standalone theory of harm — an entirely new analytical category that the Commission can deploy against mergers where competitive pressure between operators to invest in networks itself has market value. For a mobile 4→3 deal, this is the new battleground: even where the merged entity commits to maintaining capex, the Commission can argue that eliminating an independent network builder removes an investment stimulus the market benefited from.

For active deals, the practical read is positive on net: a clearer, more predictable single framework replaces two aging guidance documents, substantially reducing regulatory uncertainty in complex multi-jurisdiction transactions. The **DT / T-Mobile US** deal — requiring simultaneous FCC, DOJ, and EC clearance — benefits specifically from the extended investment horizon on the EU leg.

Public consultation closes **June 26, 2026**; final adoption is expected **Q4 2026 or early 2027**.

**Watch over the next 6–18 months:** Stakeholder responses from incumbent telcos and national competition authorities to the June 26 consultation — specifically whether the Commission addresses 4→3 mobile market consolidation explicitly in final text. Whether the "loss of investment competition" theory is deployed in any active review. And how the updated framework shapes the EU leg of the Deutsche Telekom / T-Mobile US combination, which is the most complex multi-regulator telecom transaction in the current cycle.
articles.summary: The European Commission published its first comprehensive merger guidelines overhaul since 2004, abandoning the rigid 2-year benefit horizon that made infrastructure consolidation analytically difficult to defend. The change is structurally favorable for every major active European telecom deal — SFR, the reported Deutsche Telekom/T-Mobile US combination — while a new 'loss of investment competition' theory creates a countervailing lever the Commission can apply.

articles.title: Europe's Data Centre Clean Power Pipeline Is Breaking Down
articles.subtitle: Offshore wind PPAs for data centres collapsed to 100 MW in Q1 2026 — the mechanism supposed to power Europe's AI build-out is in structural retreat.
articles.body_md:
**Rystad Energy** has published data confirming a structural fracture in the European clean energy procurement model for data centres. European data centre PPA volumes fell **38%** — from **4.2 GW** in 2024 to **2.6 GW** in 2025. In Q1 2026, the offshore wind segment — projected as the primary clean power vehicle for European data centres through the mid-2030s — contracted just **100 MW**. In 2024 the same segment delivered **1.35 GW**; in 2025, **0.5 GW**. The wider European PPA market across all sectors has seen deal count fall **60% year-on-year** and contracted capacity fall **40% versus 2024**.

The collapse is supply-side, not demand-side.

## Three Structural Causes

First, offshore wind project delivery delays have removed large-volume contracts from the available pipeline — developers cannot offer capacity they do not yet have, and European offshore wind construction timelines have slipped materially across the North Sea and Baltic. Second, a pricing standoff has emerged: falling capture rates and rising negative wholesale electricity price hours erode wind and solar economics in spot markets, forcing developers to ask above-market PPA prices that hyperscalers and co-location operators will not accept. Third, data centre operators are pivoting toward nuclear and hybrid baseload structures. **Amazon**, **Google**, and **Microsoft** have all signed nuclear-linked deals in the US; European equivalents remain constrained by fleet age, regulation, and geography.

## The Geography of the Alternative

Where European data centres cannot procure wind PPAs, they are moving toward power-surplus markets with baseload alternatives. Norwegian and Swedish hydro provides the closest European parallel to the nuclear baseload logic driving US demand. **Nscale**'s 230MW Narvik campus (Edition 13) is the clearest example: the Narvik thesis is explicitly a hydro-anchored clean power structure, not a PPA-dependent one. **HSCALE**'s Milan campuses (Edition 13) reflect the alternative approach — accepting that energy procurement certainty in FLAP-D markets requires a generation co-investment, as the **CRU** generation obligation in Ireland (Edition 10) now codifies by regulation.

For infrastructure investors, the implication is asset pricing: a data centre without long-term power procurement certainty is structurally mispriced in a market where contractable clean power supply is shrinking relative to demand. The **EDCA**'s **€176B** European DC buildout forecast (Edition 13) assumes capacity that has no confirmed clean power basis across significant portions of the legacy-FLAP geography.

**Watch over the next 6–18 months:** European utility Q2 2026 earnings for PPA pipeline confirmation or further deterioration; UK Contracts for Difference auction outcomes as a proxy for offshore wind economics; and whether any EU member state launches a preferential clean-power data centre tariff regime to address the investment gap between declared buildout ambition and available contracted supply.
articles.summary: European data centre PPA volumes fell 38% from 4.2 GW in 2024 to 2.6 GW in 2025, with offshore wind deals collapsing to just 100 MW in Q1 2026 — from 1.35 GW in 2024. The retreat is structural: project delays, a developer-operator pricing standoff, and operator pivot toward nuclear and hydro baseload have broken the mechanism that was supposed to power Europe's AI infrastructure build-out.

articles.title: Brussels Commits €347M to Submarine Cable Security — June 30 Funding Deadline Open Now
articles.subtitle: Two CEF Digital calls totalling €200M close June 30, with precedent 50% EU co-funding available for projects on Europe's 13 priority cable routes.
articles.body_md:
The **European Commission** has opened two **Connecting Europe Facility (CEF) Digital** funding calls totalling **€200M**, with a **June 30, 2026** submission deadline. Combined with a separately opened **Baltic Sea emergency repair call** of **€20M** (February 5, 2026), total EU submarine cable commitment for 2026–2027 reaches **€347M** — the most substantial European public investment in submarine cable infrastructure to date.

The architecture is operationally specific. The **€180M backbone call** targets Europe's **13 Cable Projects of European Interest** — the highest-traffic, highest-consequence links in the European network map — with the explicit goal of diversifying supply paths and hardening existing routes. The **€20M smart cable call** funds real-time infrastructure monitoring upgrades across the same priority network. The **€20M Baltic Sea call** does not fund new cable construction: it funds emergency repair capability, a direct response to documented Baltic cable incidents since late 2024 attributed to anchor drag and, in some cases, suspected deliberate action.

## Governance Layer: The Cable Security Toolbox

Alongside the funding calls, the Commission released the **Cable Security Toolbox** — standardised EU-level threat assessment and resilience protocols for cable operators and member states. The Toolbox creates a EU-wide cable resilience standard without requiring bilateral negotiation between individual operators and member states, reducing the coordination overhead that has slowed European cable security responses.

## Timing and the Geopolitical Context

The package arrives as the **subsea-cable-disruption** thread has reframed cable resilience from a technical to a geopolitical priority. **17 cables** remain disrupted via the Red Sea corridor with no repair timeline. **Iran** has formalised a permit and fee mandate for **7 Hormuz cables** — including **Falcon** and **GBI** (TeleGeography confirmed). **Italy** acquired **TIM Sparkle** for **€700M** (EC-cleared, Edition 13), taking direct state control of Mediterranean routing. The EU funding response addresses the European network dimension: Baltic and North Sea resilience, backbone route diversity, and repair preparedness — distinct from the geopolitical chokepoints at Red Sea and Hormuz, but related in strategic logic.

For operators and investors in European cable infrastructure, the June 30 deadline is a live funding opportunity. The **GlobalConnect Kattegat cable** (Edition 12) established the co-funding precedent: **50% of eligible project costs**, with the EU contributing **€5.9M** of a **€11.9M** investment. Projects on the **13-priority-cable list** — covering Baltic, North Sea, and Mediterranean routes — may apply under the same framework.

**Watch over the next 6–18 months:** Which projects receive approval from the €180M backbone call; whether the €20M Baltic Sea emergency repair fund catalyses a consortium among Baltic rim operators (**Nokia**/**Alcatel Submarine Networks**, **Prysmian**); and whether the Cable Security Toolbox is adopted as binding EU guidance or remains voluntary for member state implementation.
articles.summary: The EU has committed €347M across three submarine cable security funding calls, with €200M in live CEF Digital calls closing June 30 — open to operators on Europe's 13 Cable Projects of European Interest at up to 50% co-funding. The package adds a Cable Security Toolbox and emergency Baltic repair funding, arriving as Red Sea and Hormuz disruptions make cable resilience a geopolitical priority.

articles.title: Moody's Projects $785B Hyperscaler Capex for 2026 — $1 Trillion in Sight by 2027
articles.subtitle: A $60B upward revision from prior consensus, combined with a 50% YoY surge in DC optical interconnect orders, confirms the AI supercycle is accelerating.
articles.body_md:
**Moody's Ratings** has revised its 2026 combined hyperscaler capital expenditure projection to **$785B** — a **$60B** upward revision from the **$725B** figure DII tracked through company-level guidance aggregation at Q1 2026 earnings (Edition 10). For 2027, Moody's projects hyperscaler capex approaching **$1 trillion**, implying compound growth of approximately **30% per annum** from the ~**$410B** 2025 baseline. This is a formal credit-rating agency endorsement of a spending trajectory that infrastructure investors have been pricing into asset valuations for 18 months.

Individual 2026 company guidance is unchanged: **Microsoft** $190B, **Amazon** $200B, **Alphabet** $180–190B, **Meta** $125–145B.

## What Drove the $60B Revision

The gap between corporate guidance and Moody's aggregate is not a single company change — no hyperscaler materially altered its full-year 2026 guidance between Q1 earnings and the Moody's publication. The revision reflects Moody's own analytical aggregation incorporating supply-chain data, facility construction spend, and committed capital not yet visible in corporate filings. This is a meaningful distinction: Moody's is capturing economic activity occurring between the balance sheet and the income statement — equipment orders, land acquisition, and contracted construction — that standard earnings disclosures do not fully reflect until delivery.

The most actionable signal for European infrastructure operators sits alongside the headline: cloud provider **optical transport equipment purchases for DC interconnect** increased **50% year-on-year** in Q1 2026. Optical interconnect equipment is a leading indicator — it precedes compute deployment — and a 50% single-quarter increase confirms that AI data workloads are consuming backbone bandwidth at rates materially outpacing the build-out assumptions priced into 2023 and 2024 infrastructure investments.

## Private Capital Is Now Cross-Platform

The private capital stack tracking the hyperscaler capex thesis has become structurally cross-platform. **KKR Helix** ($10B+ committed, Edition 12) targets NVIDIA GPU-centric infrastructure. **Blackstone**'s Google TPU joint venture ($25B with leverage, Edition 13) targets proprietary AI silicon. **AIP/Aligned** ($40B, Edition 5) targets DC real estate. Aggregate institutional private capital committed to AI infrastructure platforms now exceeds **$75B** — meaning capital will absorb multiple forms of hyperscaler off-balance-sheet demand simultaneously, not concentrating in a single asset class.

For European fibre backbone operators — **GlobalConnect** (€8B sale process ongoing), **BT Openreach**, **Orange wholesale** — the optical interconnect surge means sustained hyperscaler procurement demand at increasing volumes. The $785B capex figure, if confirmed by Q2 earnings, will pull forward procurement timelines and increase per-unit pricing pressure on limited European connectivity capacity.

**Watch over the next 6–18 months:** Q2 2026 hyperscaler earnings for any guidance revision beyond $785B; European DC land and power pricing as leading indicators of hyperscaler acquisition pace; and whether Moody's or other rating agencies adjust hyperscaler credit outlooks as capex-to-free-cash-flow ratios reach historically elevated levels.
articles.summary: Moody's Ratings has revised 2026 combined hyperscaler capex to $785B — $60B above prior consensus — and projects spending approaching $1 trillion by 2027. A simultaneous 50% year-on-year surge in cloud provider optical transport equipment orders signals AI workloads are consuming European backbone bandwidth faster than the infrastructure was built to handle.

articles.title: Ireland's Data Centre Policy Faces High Court Challenge — Connection Approvals at Risk
articles.subtitle: Friends of the Irish Environment, Friends of the Earth, and ClientEarth obtained leave April 28 to challenge the CRU's 80%-renewable requirement as legally insufficient.
articles.body_md:
The **Irish High Court** granted leave on **April 28, 2026** for a judicial review of the **Commission for Regulation of Utilities (CRU)**'s data centre connection policy — the framework introduced in December 2025 (Edition 10) requiring all new connections of **1 MVA** or greater to build matching generation capacity, participate in wholesale electricity markets, and source at least **80% Irish-origin renewables** within six years of grid energisation. An active legal challenge is now proceeding, introducing a concrete risk that has not been priced into the investment narrative for Ireland's data centre market.

## The Challengers and Their Argument

The claimants are **Friends of the Irish Environment**, **Friends of the Earth Ireland**, and **ClientEarth** — the same coalition that has previously secured Irish High Court orders against planning and energy decisions on climate grounds. Their legal argument is specific: the CRU policy permits up to **20%** of data centre electricity from non-renewable sources; the challengers contend this violates Irish and EU climate law and is incompatible with Ireland's statutory climate targets.

If successful, the court could order the CRU to revise the policy — potentially eliminating the 20% non-renewable allowance, imposing a 100% renewable standard, or — the highest-consequence outcome — suspending new connection approvals pending a revised CRU decision. That interim scenario would affect operators and investors with pending connection applications immediately.

## The Paradox: Already the Most Demanding Regime in Europe

**Ireland**'s total data centre load stands at approximately **800 MW** — **21% of national electricity demand**. The CRU framework was already the most demanding data centre grid connection regime in Europe before the legal challenge: the generation obligation requirement converts every new operator into an energy infrastructure developer, substantially repricing Ireland's tier-1 market entry cost and sharpening the competitive advantage of Nordic markets without equivalent obligations (Edition 10).

A successful legal challenge would tighten this framework further, or invalidate it entirely. The challengers' track record is credible; Irish courts have applied climate legislation strictly and in alignment with EU frameworks in prior energy and planning cases. The specific argument — that even 80% renewables with a 20% non-renewable tolerance is legally insufficient — is a high evidentiary bar, but not an implausible one under Irish and EU climate law as currently interpreted.

The system operators' green energy parks engagement process, required by **March 31, 2026** per CRU instructions, has not been publicly confirmed, adding procedural uncertainty alongside the legal uncertainty.

**Watch over the next 6–18 months:** High Court hearing timeline — typically 12–18 months from leave grant for substantive proceedings; whether the CRU pre-empts a ruling by voluntarily amending the policy to a stricter renewable standard; and whether the judicial review deters final investment decisions at two or three major Irish data centre projects currently in site selection, particularly those whose pro-forma financial models assume a 20% non-renewable allowance remains available.
articles.summary: The Irish High Court granted leave April 28 for judicial review of the CRU's data centre connection policy, which already requires 80% Irish-origin renewables and matching generation build. Challengers — Friends of the Irish Environment, Friends of the Earth Ireland, and ClientEarth — argue the 20% non-renewable allowance violates Irish and EU climate law, creating risk that new connection approvals could be suspended pending a revised policy.
